title: Zone Training and Heart Rate: A Practical Guide
seo_title: Zone Training and Heart Rate: A Practical Guide for Runners
meta_description: What heart-rate zones are, why most runners' easy runs are actually run too hard, and how to estimate zones without lab testing -- honestly.
dek: Heart-rate zones are a useful tool for a very specific job: catching the runs that feel easy but aren't, and the runs that feel controlled but are secretly too hard.

sections.heading: What Heart-Rate Zones Actually Are
paragraphs: A heart-rate zone system divides the range between resting and maximum heart rate into bands -- usually three to five -- that correspond to broad categories of training effort, from very easy to maximal. The point isn't the exact number of zones a given system uses; it's that zones convert a fuzzy feeling like "easy" or "hard" into a number a runner can actually check mid-run, rather than relying purely on how a pace feels, which can be misleading on a given day.

Zones are most useful as a classification tool for a training week as a whole: they let a runner see, in aggregate, roughly how much of the week was spent at low intensity versus how much drifted into a harder, more moderate effort -- exactly the kind of training-intensity distribution that research on recreational runners has studied directly[1].

sections.heading: Why Most "Easy" Runs Are Actually Run Too Hard
paragraphs: One of the most commonly repeated observations in endurance coaching is that recreational runners' easy runs tend to drift into a moderate, in-between effort rather than staying genuinely easy -- and the training-intensity distribution research bears this out: runners who deliberately structured their easy running to sit at low intensity, keeping only a small share of weekly volume genuinely hard, were following a pattern consistent with how endurance athletes are generally studied to train, in contrast to runners who spend the bulk of their week in a moderate, neither-easy-nor-hard zone[1].

This drift happens for understandable reasons: an easy run that feels comfortable can still creep up in heart rate on a hot day, in a group run with faster friends, or simply because a runner is fitter than their training plan assumes and "easy" no longer feels like enough of a workout. None of those are good reasons to run an easy day hard -- they're exactly the situations a heart-rate zone check is useful for catching.

sections.heading: Estimating Zones Without a Lab
paragraphs: Heart-rate zones are usually set as percentages of maximum heart rate, and most runners never lab-test their true max -- they estimate it with a formula instead. The long-standing "220 minus age" formula is the most familiar, but a widely cited study that reviewed data across hundreds of studies and thousands of subjects found it systematically inaccurate, particularly underestimating maximum heart rate in older adults, and proposed a revised formula -- 208 minus 0.7 times age -- as a more accurate population-level estimate[2].

Even the revised formula comes with an important honesty caveat: any age-based formula is a population average, and individual maximum heart rates vary meaningfully from person to person at the same age -- the original research behind the revised formula itself reports a real margin of error. In practice, that means a formula-derived zone should be treated as a starting estimate to refine with lived experience, not a precise number to chase on a watch.

sections.heading: Connecting Zones Back to Easy Pace
paragraphs: Heart-rate zones and the talk test covered in this site's guide to easy pace are answering the same underlying question -- is this run actually easy? -- from two different angles: one physiological, one perceptual. Used together, they're more reliable than either alone, because a heart-rate number can be thrown off by heat, dehydration, caffeine, or stress on a given day, while the talk test can be thrown off by a runner simply pushing through discomfort out of habit.

When the two disagree -- heart rate reading high on a run that still feels conversational, for instance -- that's usually a signal worth listening to rather than dismissing, particularly in hot, humid conditions where heart rate at a given pace runs higher than it would in cooler weather. Treating zones as one input among several, rather than the single source of truth, is what makes heart-rate training useful in practice rather than a rigid number to obey regardless of context.

faqs.question: What are heart-rate training zones?
faqs.answer: Heart-rate zones divide the range from resting to maximum heart rate into bands, usually three to five, that correspond to broad training-effort categories from very easy to maximal. They turn a subjective feeling like "easy" into a number a runner can check during a run.

faqs.question: Why do coaches say runners train their easy runs too hard?
faqs.answer: Easy runs commonly drift into a moderate, in-between effort rather than staying genuinely easy -- from heat, group-run pace pressure, or improving fitness outpacing an old pace target. Research on training-intensity distribution in recreational runners supports keeping easy runs deliberately low-intensity rather than moderate.

faqs.question: How accurate is the "220 minus age" max heart rate formula?
faqs.answer: Not very -- research reviewing data across hundreds of studies found it systematically inaccurate, especially in older adults, and proposed a revised formula (208 minus 0.7 times age) instead. Even revised formulas carry a real margin of error, since individual max heart rate varies meaningfully person to person.
